scenes.headline: Strings & f-strings
scenes.subtitle: Working with text the modern way
scenes.narration: Text is everywhere in data engineering, from file paths to log messages, and strings are how Python handles all of it.

scenes.headline: Handy string skills
items: Methods like upper, strip and split
scenes.narration: Slicing lets you grab a section of a string by position, which is handy for pulling fixed-width fields apart. A rich set of methods such as upper, strip and split cleans and reshapes text with a single call. F-strings let you drop variables directly into text, making messages easy to build. And because strings are immutable, every method returns a new string rather than changing the original in place.

scenes.headline: Building messages with f-strings
scenes.code:
table = 'events'
rows = 4200
msg = f'Loaded {rows:,} rows into {table}'
print(msg)
scenes.narration: We start with a table name and a row count. The f-string embeds both variables right inside the text using curly braces, and the comma inside the braces formats the number with thousands separators. The result is a clean, readable log line printed in a single step.

scenes.headline: f-string versus older formatting
scenes.narration: F-strings keep the value right next to the text, so you can read the final message at a glance, and they are also the fastest option. The older format method and percent style still work and appear in legacy code, but they push the values away from where they land. For new code, f-strings are almost always the clearer choice.

scenes.headline: A common cleaning pipeline
scenes.narration: A typical text cleanup starts with raw, messy input. You strip the surrounding whitespace, lowercase it so comparisons behave consistently, and then split it on a delimiter into separate fields. Chaining these string methods handles the majority of everyday parsing.

scenes.text: Reach for f-strings to build readable, formatted text; they are clearer and faster than older approaches.
scenes.narration: The takeaway is to reach for f-strings whenever you build text, since they keep your code concise, readable and fast.
